title: Catalogue, search, and saved discovery
summary: Trace provider results through profile policy, deliberate search interactions, and account-owned history. The target architecture is backend-agnostic.
body:
One public model, several content paths

A feature asks a public service for StreamCoreContent. Runtime owns authorization and enforcement; the selected provider fetches and maps its catalogue. Home, details, recommendations, trending, library snapshots, and playback sources must all respect the current authorized profile. A hidden card is therefore not the only protection. Calling details or playback directly still goes through SDK checks.

Read the home and details paths in order

  1. RuntimeHomeService.getCollections enters withAuthorizedProfile. The session supplies the authorized profile and its account's provider services.
  2. The home provider returns collections. Runtime filters each collection's content with contentPolicy.isContentAllowed. It preserves collection metadata and does not remove rows merely because filtering leaves them empty.
  3. getDetails first rejects a blank content ID. Inside the same authorization guard it loads details, propagates a provider failure, and returns Unauthorized if the returned content fails policy.
  4. Recommendations and trending pass successful lists through the session's shared filtering function. Session guards also check whether the captured authorization remains current when work finishes.

These are domain rules, so moving a screen or introducing a new platform does not move enforcement into a composable. Row placement, display limits, focus, and loading presentation remain application choices. A provider may filter upstream too; that does not remove runtime's responsibility to enforce the public operation.

What TMDB policy actually means

The TMDB reference provider uses isKidsProfile and TMDB's adult flag. Its catalogue repositories request or filter adult content according to includeAdult = !profile.isKidsProfile. The shared policy implementation in TmdbSdk allows non-kids profiles directly. For a kids profile it parses the content ID as a movie ID, fetches movie details, and permits the item only when adult is false. An invalid movie ID is denied; a failed lookup propagates as a provider operation error.

Do not teach this as “content rating must be below the profile's numeric parental level.” The model contains certification labels and numeric levels, but the current TMDB policy does not compare those numbers. Another provider can implement different rules behind the same policy contract.

The fresh lookup also matters for saved snapshots: previously saved content can become disallowed. The TMDB contract test saves an item for a kids profile, changes the fixture's adult flag, then expects details and source resolution to fail and My List to omit it. This is policy applied to previously obtained data, not just a search request parameter. Kids-profile filtering can perform additional provider requests; do not assume a saved-list read is necessarily network-free.

Search is a query plus an interaction

SearchQueryNormalizer trims the ends and collapses each whitespace run to one space. It preserves letter case. Searchability requires at least 3 characters after normalization. Runtime checks the search capability and authorized context before returning an empty list for a short query; “too short” is not permission to skip context checks. Valid text reaches the provider in normalized form.

Call or interactionHistory behavior
search(..., Typing)Search results only; no history checkpoint.
Submitted or RecentSelectedRecords only after successful, policy-filtered, nonempty results.
displayedResultsRecords a non-typing interaction with already displayed nonempty results without querying again.
resultSelectedRecords the query associated with opening a result.
recordHistoryExplicit history operation; normalizes and ignores too-short text. Do not duplicate an interaction already recorded above.

A failed history checkpoint does not replace a successful catalogue result from search. Cancellation still propagates, and the final authorization check still applies. The explicit history methods return their own result, so callers can distinguish a failed history action. Search and search-history capabilities are separate. History stores at most 5 queries per partition, newest first; adding a case-insensitive duplicate moves the newest spelling to the front. Removing a query also compares case-insensitively.

Page limits and duplicate requests are different concerns

The current public search API returns a list and accepts no page token. TMDB uses its API's default page 1, filters adult results, takes at most 20 search results, and maps them without a catalogue-ID deduplication pass. Trending takes at most 6. Do not mistake these limits for a cross-provider paging contract.

The application's SearchViewModel separately debounces typing by 300 ms, delays the loading skeleton by 150 ms, cancels superseded work, and deduplicates queued queries using normalized lowercase keys. Submit and recent selection execute immediately; submitting an already displayed query can call displayedResults instead of repeating the catalogue request. Its 10-query result cache supports Network/Timeout fallback. Those UI timing and cache rules are not delays imposed by SearchService.

Reading and changing exercise

Trace “ alien world ” through Typing, Submitted, and a repeated submit after results are visible. Identify the normalized string, the one provider request that UI deduplication can avoid, and the history operation that still occurs. Then sketch a change from five history entries to eight: change the storage retention rule and its focused tests, not the search debounce. For a new paging feature, start with a deliberate public result/request contract and provider capability behavior; changing TMDB's internal page alone cannot expose navigation to consumers.

quiz.question: A successful Submitted search returns allowed results, but saving its history fails. What should the caller receive?
options: The successful catalogue result, subject to cancellation and the final context check.
A successful empty list because history could not be saved.
A storage failure instead of the catalogue result.
quiz.explanation: RuntimeSearchService deliberately keeps successful catalogue results when the history checkpoint fails. Explicit history operations expose their own failures, and cancellation/context loss are still enforced.

title: Playback sources, events, and resume
kicker: One service, one recorder per playback
summary: Separate media resolution from saved progress, then walk the recorder's exact cadence, completion, and failure behavior.
body:
Three entry points with different jobs

RuntimePlaybackService owns source resolution, progress operations, and progress-event handling together. The application owns the player engine and its rendering. The service's private inner ProgressRecorder keeps one request, captured authorization, mutex, and periodic bucket. There is no separate progress-only runtime interface or callback factory between library observation and this service.

Entry pointResponsibility
resolveSource(request)Validate the request, authorize access, refresh details, enforce policy, and ask the provider for playable media.
updateProgress(entry)Apply direct progress validation and resume policy, then upsert or remove the saved entry.
createProgressRecorder(...).reportEvent(...)Translate player events into progress operations with captured authorization and event-specific cadence.

Use the recorder for player callbacks. Reporting an event already performs its required storage operation; calling updateProgress for the same sample would duplicate work and bypass the recorder's intended cadence. “Recorder” here means recording progress events, not recording audio or video.

Source resolution does not trust a stale card snapshot

  1. An unsupported playback capability returns Unsupported. A blank content ID or mismatched snapshot ID returns validation failure.
  2. The session authorizes the request's profile. The service loads fresh details using the captured account's details provider.
  3. Content policy checks the fresh content. A stale activation is rejected before asking the playback provider for a source.
  4. The provider receives a request copied with the refreshed snapshot and returns StreamCorePlaybackMedia. Session guards translate provider failures and prevent an obsolete result from becoming current.

The player then prepares its application-owned session. In the current TMDB reference implementation, playable media is explicitly opted-in demo media; catalogue ownership and progress identity still belong to the requested content. The player uses the resolved media title for display while the recorder retains the original request's content identity.

Resume policy and event cadence are independent

A position is resumable only when duration is positive, position is at least 30,000 ms, and position / duration is strictly below 0.95. For a 100-second item, 29,999 ms is too early, 30,000 ms is eligible, 94,999 ms is eligible, and 95,000 ms is complete for retention purposes. Direct progress updates remove an existing entry when it is no longer resumable. They also reject a blank ID, mismatched snapshot ID, or negative update timestamp and enforce profile/content policy before storage.

The recorder divides the position by 10,000 ms to form an integer bucket. Its initial bucket comes from the initial resume position. A periodic sample attempts persistence only if its bucket is strictly greater than the last attempted bucket. This is a position-based rule, not a wall-clock timer or “save every ten seconds since the previous write.”

EventExact behavior
CompletedRemoves progress immediately, even when duration is unknown.
Other event with duration ≤ 0Returns success without changing data or the periodic bucket.
PeriodicSkips same/earlier buckets; advances a new bucket before persistence.
CheckpointAttempts immediately, without reading or changing the cadence bucket.

Suppose playback resumes at 45 seconds: bucket 4 is already accounted for. Samples at 45 and 49.999 seconds do nothing; 50 seconds attempts bucket 5. If that attempt fails, a 59-second periodic sample does not retry. A 35-second checkpoint can retry explicitly, but leaves bucket 5 unchanged; periodic work resumes only upon reaching bucket 6 at 60 seconds. A seek backwards does not reset the periodic gate.

Unknown duration intentionally differs between APIs. A recorder checkpoint with duration zero preserves existing progress because the player may not know duration yet. A direct updateProgress with duration zero applies resume policy and removes the entry. Completed removes regardless of duration.

Each recorder serializes reports with its own mutex, so two recorders from one shared service do not share cadence. Ordinary thrown event-processing exceptions become StreamCoreError.Storage; a CancellationException is rethrown. A failed periodic attempt remains consumed and schedules no automatic retry. A later checkpoint or higher bucket is a separate attempt. The captured authorization never silently follows a newly selected profile.

How progress becomes Continue Watching

The preferences store keeps the newest 50 entries per account/profile partition, ordered by updatedAtMillis. It strips nested contentSnapshot.playbackProgress before serialization. Reads filter by the physical partition, then runtime applies content policy and restores the public profile ID. RuntimeLibraryService combines membership entries with the actual playback service's observation, using the same captured authorization for both. It creates Continue Watching cards with a fresh progress decoration; liked/My List cards have no progress decoration.

Player exit must remain usable when saving fails

PlayerViewModel creates one player session from its factory and closes it in onCleared. Preparation reads saved progress, resolves media, creates a recorder, and prepares the engine. A failed progress read falls back to zero; a source failure presents sanitized application-owned text. Playing engine updates send Periodic events; completion sends Completed. Pause, seek, scrub, background/PiP changes, and exit send checkpoints at their relevant interaction points.

Back first closes an open settings panel. Otherwise it marks navigation pending, cancels preparation, pauses the prepared session, awaits a checkpoint, and emits one NavigateBack effect. A returned storage failure does not prevent navigation or turn controls into a playback error. Cancellation is still cancellation, not a successful exit checkpoint. Existing tests cover failed saves, failed removals, unknown duration, and one-time navigation.

Reading and changing exercise

Predict the writes for a recorder initialized at 45 seconds receiving Periodic at 49.999, 50, and 50.001 seconds, then Checkpoint at 35 seconds, then Completed with zero duration. The expected attempts are one periodic write, one checkpoint write, and one removal. Now consider changing completion to 90%: update the public policy, the preferences store's duplicated retention threshold, focused boundary tests, and explanatory UI where applicable. Do not change the ten-second bucket unless cadence is separately part of the requirement.

quiz.question: A Periodic save at 40 seconds fails. What happens at 49 seconds, followed by a Checkpoint at 35 seconds?
options: Both retry because the previous save failed.
49 seconds is skipped; the checkpoint attempts a save without resetting the bucket.
quiz.explanation: Bucket 4 was consumed before the failed save. A same-bucket Periodic report is skipped. Checkpoint bypasses cadence and leaves the bucket unchanged.

title: Persistence, partitions, and storage availability
summary: See how logical profile data reaches platform storage, survives restarts, and stays isolated by authenticated account and profile.
body:
Storage sits behind runtime services

Library membership, search history, and playback progress are SDK-local responsibilities. Their narrow stores live beside preferences implementations under runtime.storage.library, .search, and .playback. Provider factories assemble them through PreferencesSdkStorage and supply the resulting SdkLocalRepositories to runtime. Features consume public services; they do not receive raw DataStore, serialized preferences, or store interfaces.

Authentication persistence remains provider-owned. The platform storage bundle supplies an auth/context store, but the provider owns credential/session protocols and its own serialized authentication state. Runtime additionally persists selected-profile context and checks auth/context storage availability before authentication workflows. A common physical storage bundle does not erase those ownership boundaries.

The “profile ID” inside a store is a partition key

Public operations accept the logical profile ID. RuntimeSession.storageKey derives the physical key from the captured authorized account and profile. accountStorageKey prefixes sdk2: and length-frames four fields in order: backend, storage namespace, account ID, and profile ID. Each field becomes its character length, a colon, and the original field value. Framing avoids ambiguous concatenations when identifiers contain delimiters or Unicode.

Thus two accounts with the same profile ID cannot share history or progress. Backend and namespace further separate installations/environments. This key is an ownership encoding, not encryption, a credential, or evidence of authentication. The session supplies authenticated identity; callers do not gain authority by constructing a matching-looking string. Public progress reads convert the stored key back to the requested logical profile ID before returning models.

Library: two memberships, one saved snapshot

setLiked and setInMyList change independent memberships on the same content entry. RuntimeLibraryService captures authorization and reads its clock once per call. It checks capability, content ID, timestamp, authorized profile, and content policy before invoking the real LibraryStore with the account/profile partition. The operation returns that store result; it does not merely prepare a command for the client to execute later.

Trace one item's membership changes

  1. Like an item at time 10: likedAtMillis = 10, with no My List timestamp.
  2. Add it to My List at time 20: keep the like timestamp and set addedToMyListAtMillis = 20. Both memberships share one compact content snapshot.
  3. Like it again at time 30 with an updated title: preserve the original like timestamp, but refresh the snapshot from the supplied content. Repeated inclusion is idempotent for membership time, not a guarantee that metadata stays unchanged.
  4. Unlike it: clear only the like timestamp and retain the existing snapshot and My List membership. Removal does not refresh the snapshot from its input. Removing the remaining membership deletes the entry; removing a nonexistent entry is a no-op.

The preferences transaction decodes, changes, and encodes the current payload atomically, preserving concurrent updates to the other membership. Unchanged entries skip rewriting. Store observation sorts by the latest of the two membership timestamps descending, then content ID ascending. The public library independently sorts Liked by like time and My List by addition time. An item can therefore occupy different positions in the two rows.

Observe a library, not three unrelated subscriptions

observe captures one grant and combines allowed membership entries with RuntimePlaybackService.observeProgress using that same grant. Continue Watching preserves progress order and adds progress decoration; Liked and My List explicitly clear it. observeContentState reads the two membership booleans without combining progress.

Within the combined result, a library failure takes precedence over a progress failure; an unchanged valid grant is still required by the final session check. A thrown storage error terminates its inner store collection after emitting failure. Simply repairing storage does not restart that collection: create and collect a fresh observation. The focused test first exposes the library failure, then the progress failure, and finally proves recovery through a new observation. A new activation also requires a freshly captured observation.

Know the serialized shape before changing it

Preference keyPayload and semantics
library_jsonAn object with version metadata and entriesByProfile. Entries store a reduced content snapshot plus independent liked/My List timestamps.
recent_searches_jsonAn object with queriesByProfile. Each partition retains five strings, newest first, deduplicated case-insensitively.
entries_jsonA flat list of playback entries; each entry's profileId holds the physical partition. Retains the newest 50 per partition.
sdk_selected_profile. + account keyAccount-scoped selected-profile value using an empty profile segment in the key. Empty string is a deliberate cleared-selection sentinel.

Library snapshots retain card metadata, not full details: their reconstructed content has an empty description/cast, null row, and null progress. Enabling a membership that already exists preserves its original membership timestamp; liked and My List timestamps remain independent. Removing the last membership removes the entry. The library flow sorts memberships into their own rows and derives Continue Watching from progress separately.

The library serializer currently defaults its version field to 1. The authentication storage check writes sdk_context_schema = "2" in auth/context preferences. That current context-format marker also exercises storage availability; it does not dispatch saved-data conversion. Read the actual decoder before changing fields or defaults.

Production assembly wraps stores in ErrorMappingPreferencesStore and enables failure reporting for search/progress. I/O errors become storage failures; serialization failures become Parsing in suspend operations; search-history/progress observations currently map uncategorized decode failures to Storage. Do not infer production behavior from a repository's default reportFailures = false constructor parameter: factories explicitly opt in. Browser storage also avoids replacing corrupt preferences with empty values.

Persistent and InMemory are the current modes

StreamCorePersistenceMode has exactly Persistent and InMemory. Persistent means local platform-backed state; it does not mean backend synchronization. InMemory creates four independent memory preferences stores with serialized updates, useful for isolated consumers/tests. A Local/Backend saved-data mode and synchronization semantics remain deferred; do not advertise Backend as an existing enum value or capability.

Android's factory creates four DataStores under application storage: auth, library, search history, and playback progress. Filenames use hexadecimal encodings of the auth name, backend, and namespace. Providers and applications share these current namespaced defaults. There is no alternate historical filename mode. A process-local owner registry rejects a second live owner for those canonical files. Closing storage cancels its scope; the owner reservation releases when that job completes.

Browser construction uses the same logical bundle over WebLocalStorage, or WebSessionStorage when the host selects session fallback. Its owner keys include local/session mode. The web application's startup probe and fallback logic decide whether to retry recoverable storage failures using session storage and display a warning. Session state is lost when the tab closes; this is not equivalent to durable local storage. Non-storage startup failures are not automatically solved by fallback.

Check storage without importing old development data

There are no shipped-data compatibility requirements. The SDK does not convert old application payloads, map their owners, create backups/quarantine, or select old application filenames. Existing development files and browser keys remain untouched and are not imported. Current-store ownership comes from the authenticated account and authorized profile supplied by the session.

Before restoration, login, or logout, RuntimeAuthService.ensureContextStorageAvailable() invokes SdkLocalRepositories.checkContextStorage. Production preferences assembly writes sdk_context_schema = "2" through the auth/context store. A successful check sets contextStorageChecked; failure returns to the caller and permits retry. This keeps browser startup's persistent-to-session fallback available before login. Library, history, and progress are decoded or written only when their ordinary operations run, with their existing error handling.

The selected-profile value remains context metadata, not authorization. A fresh client must enter a profile even when a stored reference exists. Successful logout clears authentication and active context while retaining the authenticated account's saved data; closing releases resources without erasure.

Reading and changing exercise

Inspect the restart tests and explain how accounts A and B with the same profile ID retain separate library/history/progress. Then sketch adding a saved-data field: identify its public meaning, serialized default, ownership scope, and direct runtime/current-storage restart checks. Avoid exposing preferences types to a feature just to make the change easier.

Android host tests reopen actual binary DataStore files. The browser restart test exercises real localStorage when run in a browser, but explicitly returns early in Node when browser storage is unavailable. A passing Node case therefore does not prove browser durability. This guide links existing tests; it does not claim they were executed while authoring the chapters.

quiz.question: Why does authentication check the auth/context store before restoring or logging in?
options: To import old profile data into whichever account signs in next.
To authorize the profile remembered in storage without fresh entry.
To expose storage availability failures early so the browser host can choose session fallback.
quiz.explanation: The check probes current auth/context storage and caches success. It does not convert saved data or grant profile authorization; current saved state remains scoped to the authenticated account and profile.
